solutions.latex:
Let $A$ be the event that Benjamin wins on the first or second day. Let $W$ be the event that Benjamin wins.

$$P(\overline{W})=0.93$$

$$\begin{aligned}P(A)&=P(W)+P(\overline{W}W)\\&=0.07+0.93\times 0.07\\&=0.1351\end{aligned}$$

Hence the probability that Benjamin wins on the first or second day is 0.14.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: forming equation for probability; 1: final answer

solutions.latex:
Let $B$ be the event that Benjamin wins eventually. The sequence of probabilities that Benjamin wins on a certain day: $0.07,\ 0.93\times 0.07,\ 0.93^2\times 0.07,\ \cdots$

Forms a geometric sequence: $a=0.07,\ r=0.93$

$$P(B)>0.8$$

$$\frac{0.07(1-0.93^n)}{1-0.93}>0.8$$

$$1-0.93^n>0.8$$

$$-0.93^n>-0.2$$

$$0.93^n<0.2$$

$$n>\log_{0.93}0.2$$

$$n>\frac{\log_{10}0.2}{\log_{10}0.93}$$

$$n>22.18$$

Hence the smallest number of days is 23.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: forming equation for geometric sum; 2: significant progress in solving for n; 1: final answer

solutions.latex:
$$f(x)=-(x^2-4)(x-1)$$

$$\therefore\ f(x)=-(x^3-x^2-4x+4)$$

Considering the negative signed area for $-2\le x\le 1$:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=-\int_{-2}^{1}\left[-(x^3-x^2-4x+4)\right]dx+\int_{1}^{2}\left[-(x^3-x^2-4x+4)\right]dx\\&=\int_{-2}^{1}\left(x^3-x^2-4x+4\right)dx-\int_{1}^{2}\left(x^3-x^2-4x+4\right)dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+4x\right]_{-2}^{1}-\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+4x\right]_{1}^{2}\\&=[F(1)-F(-2)]-[F(2)-F(1)]\\&=\left(\frac{23}{12}-\frac{-28}{3}\right)-\left(\frac{4}{3}-\frac{23}{12}\right)\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\frac{71}{6}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: correct integral of f(x); 1: forming equation for area using signed areas; 1: final answer

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=-2x^3+6x^2$$

$$f''(x)=-6x^2+12x$$

Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$:

$$-2x^3+6x^2=0$$

$$-2x^2(x-3)=0$$

$$x=0\ \text{or}\ x=3$$

- When $x=0$: $f(0)=\dfrac{3}{2}$, $f''(0)=0$. Potential point of inflexion at $x=0$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&-1&0&1\\\hline f'(x)&8&0&4\\\hline m&\nearrow&-&\nearrow\end{array}$$

Hence $\left(0,1\tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

- When $x=3$: $f(3)=15$, $f''(3)=-18$, so $f''(3)<0$.

Hence $(3,15)$ is a maximum stationary point.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: correct coordinates for both stationary points; 1: correctly testing nature of both stationary points; 1: correctly stating the nature of both stationary points

solutions.latex:
Points of inflexion occur when $f''(x)=0$:

$$-6x^2+12x=0$$

$$-6x(x-2)=0$$

$$x=0\ \text{or}\ x=2$$

- Horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(0,1\tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ from part (a).
- When $x=2$: $f(2)=\dfrac{19}{2}$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&1&2&3\\\hline f''(x)&6&0&-18\end{array}$$

$\therefore$ Change in concavity at $x=0$.

Hence $\left(2,9\tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.
